entries.title: The Dark Story Behind Edgar Allan Poe’s Most Famous Photograph, Taken Four Days After a Laudanum Overdose
entries.summary: In the Halloween season, one American writer comes to mind more often than any other: Edgar Allan Poe. That owes in large part to his famously macabre tales like “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” and “The Masque of the Red Death,” written though they may have been with barely concealed contempt for their […]
entries.content:
In the Hal­loween sea­son, one Amer­i­can writer comes to mind more often than any oth­er: Edgar Allan Poe. That owes in large part to his famous­ly macabre tales like “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” and “The Masque of the Red Death,” writ­ten though they may have been with bare­ly con­cealed con­tempt for their sen­sa­tion-seek­ing mag­a­zine read­er­ship. But it also has to do with the image of the man him­self. Or rather, it has to do with one image in par­tic­u­lar: a daguerreo­type pho­to­graph tak­en on Novem­ber 9, 1848, at a Prov­i­dence stu­dio that has inspired prac­ti­cal­ly every rep­re­sen­ta­tion of Poe in pop­u­lar cul­ture since.

Known as Ulti­ma Thule, this famous por­trait was in fact just one of per­haps ten daguerreo­types for which Poe sat in his life­time. Inven­tor Louis Daguer­re’s ear­ly pho­to­graph­ic process, which used sil­ver-coat­ed cop­per plates, fas­ci­nat­ed Poe, who in an 1840 news­pa­per arti­cle called it “the most impor­tant, and per­haps the most extra­or­di­nary tri­umph of mod­ern sci­ence.” He described its prod­uct as “infi­nite­ly more accu­rate in its rep­re­sen­ta­tion than any paint­ing by human hands,” though any­one sit­ting for a pic­ture did have to sit still for min­utes on end, result­ing in not just the unsmil­ing vis­ages we asso­ciate with nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry pho­tog­ra­phy, but also in a com­bi­na­tion of dis­com­fort and slight blur­ring that can look vague­ly oth­er­world­ly.

That qual­i­ty may actu­al­ly have enhanced the aura of Ulti­ma Thule, which painter Michael J. Deas calls “the image of the trag­ic roman­tic poet: solemn, detached, con­sumed by his own wild­ly self-destruc­tive nature.” It sure­ly also made a dif­fer­ence that the por­trait was made, in the words of poet Her­vey Allen, “prob­a­bly at the very hour when he looked the worst that he had ever looked in his life.” He’d been tak­en to the stu­dio by a stranger with whom he’d spent the pre­vi­ous night binge-drink­ing. Just four days before that, he’d unsuc­cess­ful­ly attempt­ed sui­cide by lau­danum over­dose, a rash action tak­en after the rejec­tion of his mar­riage pro­pos­al by Sarah Helen Whit­man, a wid­owed poet he had­n’t known long — and who would give her suit­or’s immor­tal por­trait its Latin name, bor­rowed from his poem “Dream-Land.”

The orig­i­nal daguerreo­type, for which the stu­dio prob­a­bly paid the by-then notable, still per­pet­u­al­ly hard-up Poe to sit, remained with its mak­ers until it van­ished around 1860, and its where­abouts have remained unknown ever since. But copies have allowed gen­er­a­tion after gen­er­a­tion of read­ers to behold Poe’s trou­bled vis­age when what Whit­man called “all the stormy grandeur of that via Dolorosa had left its sullen shad­ow on his brow.” Through the drunk­en chaos and pover­ty of his life, the writer him­self could see things to come. “The con­se­quences of any new sci­en­tif­ic inven­tion will, at the present day exceed, by very much, the wildest expec­ta­tions of the most imag­i­na­tive,” he wrote, an obser­va­tion true enough of pho­tog­ra­phy 178 years ago, and no doubt even truer of what we use to make images today.

entries.title: When a Cat Co-Authored a Paper in a Leading Physics Journal (1975)
entries.summary: Back in 1975, Jack H. Hetherington, a physics professor at Michigan State University, wrote a research paper on low–temperature physics for the respected scientific journal Physical Review Letters. Before sending it off, Hetherington asked a colleague to review the paper, just to make sure it covered the right bases. What happened next Hetherington explained in the 1982 book, More Random Walks […]
entries.content:
Back in 1975, Jack H. Het­her­ing­ton, a physics pro­fes­sor at Michi­gan State Uni­ver­si­ty, wrote a research paper on low–temperature physics for the respect­ed sci­en­tif­ic jour­nal Phys­i­cal Review Let­ters. Before send­ing it off, Het­her­ing­ton asked a col­league to review the paper, just to make sure it cov­ered the right bases. What hap­pened next Het­her­ing­ton explained in the 1982 book, More Ran­dom Walks in Sci­ence:

Before I sub­mit­ted [the arti­cle], I asked a col­league to read it over and he said, ‘It’s a fine paper, but they’ll send it right back.’ He explained that that is because of the Edi­tor’s rule that the word “we” should not be used in a paper with only a sin­gle author. Chang­ing the paper to the imper­son­al seemed too dif­fi­cult now, and it was all writ­ten and typed; there­fore, after an evening’s thought, I sim­ply asked the sec­re­tary to change the title page to include the name of the fam­i­ly cat, a Siamese called Chester, sired one sum­mer by Willard (one of the few unfixed male Siamese cats in Aspen, Col­orado). I added the ini­tials F D in front of the name to stand for Felix Domes­ti­cus and thus cre­at­ed F D C Willard.

The edi­tors even­tu­al­ly accept­ed the paper, “Two‑, Three‑, and Four-Atom Exchange Effects in bcc 3 He.” And the ruse last­ed until, remem­bers Het­her­ing­ton, “a vis­i­tor [came to the uni­ver­si­ty and] asked to talk to me, and since I was unavail­able asked to talk with Willard. Every­one laughed and soon the cat was out of the bag.” (Pun sure­ly intend­ed.) Appar­ent­ly only the jour­nal edi­tors did­n’t find humor in the joke.

Above, you can see F.D.C. Willard’s sig­na­ture (a paw print) on the front page of the arti­cle. The web­site, Today­I­Found­Out, has much more on this enchant­i­ng lit­tle sto­ry.

If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

entries.title: How Vincent van Gogh’s Sister-in-Law Worked Tirelessly to Make Him Famous
entries.summary: No artist, no matter how solitary by nature, becomes a cultural phenomenon alone. That’s even true of such an isolated figure as Vincent van Gogh, whose death in obscurity at the age of 37 left open the question of who, if anyone, would vouchsafe his paintings to posterity. The support of the artist’s younger brother […]
entries.content:
No artist, no mat­ter how soli­tary by nature, becomes a cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non alone. That’s even true of such an iso­lat­ed fig­ure as Vin­cent van Gogh, whose death in obscu­ri­ty at the age of 37 left open the ques­tion of who, if any­one, would vouch­safe his paint­ings to pos­ter­i­ty. The sup­port of the artist’s younger broth­er Theo is often giv­en a good deal of cred­it for mak­ing his work pos­si­ble, and not with­out rea­son. What’s some­what less wide­ly known is that Theo, who’d long been in poor health, died less than a year after Vin­cen­t’s sui­cide. The work of ensur­ing the lat­ter’s lega­cy then fell to the for­mer’s wid­ow Johan­na Bonger — or per­haps she under­stood that if she did­n’t stew­ard it, nobody else would.

As Cindy Poh explains in the New­s­think video above, Bonger inher­it­ed a great many of van Gogh’s works and stored them away while devis­ing a plan to make them famous. Prac­ti­cal­ly going door-to-door — and some­times, it seems, lit­er­al­ly going door-to-door — she stayed engaged with the late Theo’s art-world con­tacts. She cut sweet­heart deals with muse­ums and even donat­ed art­works out­right, increas­ing their chance of pub­lic expo­sure. She orga­nized exhi­bi­tions every­where from Paris to Berlin to Lon­don to New York, the most piv­otal being one held at Ams­ter­dam’s Stedelijk Muse­um in 1905. The 484 works put on dis­play made it the largest van Gogh show in his­to­ry, a record it still holds today.

At that time, well before The Star­ry Night and Sun­flow­ers adorned cof­fee mugs in sub­ur­ban house­holds the world over, van Gogh’s art could still shock some crit­ics with its uncon­ven­tion­al­i­ty. Oth­ers, how­ev­er, showed signs of the enrap­ture­ment that Bonger must have sus­pect­ed would one day be pos­si­ble. Think­ing strate­gi­cal­ly, she pre­ferred to sell few­er pieces for high­er prices, pre­serv­ing the val­ue of his work and lim­it­ing its avail­abil­i­ty on the mar­ket. After her sec­ond hus­band’s death, she redou­bled her ded­i­ca­tion to the art that had become her life’s mis­sion, even trans­lat­ing and pub­lish­ing the hun­dreds of let­ters he’d left behind, most of which were sent to Theo. We’ve heard many artists described as mar­ried to their work, a cliché that applies well enough to Vin­cent van Gogh him­self. But to be mar­ried to one’s broth­er-in-law’s work is a rar­er thing indeed — and some­times a more impor­tant one.

entries.title: The Megaprojects That Even the Ancient Romans Couldn’t Pull Off: Rerouting the Tiber, Digging a Canal, and More
entries.summary: Some would call the United States of America the mightiest empire the world has ever known. Yet over the past half-century or so, it has shown a strange inability to build domestic infrastructure, at least at the efficiency or on the scale seen elsewhere in the world. (This will not come as news to American […]
entries.content:
Some would call the Unit­ed States of Amer­i­ca the might­i­est empire the world has ever known. Yet over the past half-cen­tu­ry or so, it has shown a strange inabil­i­ty to build domes­tic infra­struc­ture, at least at the effi­cien­cy or on the scale seen else­where in the world. (This will not come as news to Amer­i­can enthu­si­asts of high-speed rail.) Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured his­to­ry YouTu­ber Gar­rett Ryan’s take on the ques­tion of whether the U.S. is now declin­ing like the ancient Roman Empire. On a more recent video for his chan­nel Told in Stone, he’s high­light­ed the megapro­jects that even the Romans — who man­aged the Pan­theon, the Colos­se­um, and the Pont du Gard, to say noth­ing of their unique­ly long-last­ing con­crete itself — could­n’t pull off.

The Tiber may seem like a tame riv­er today, but it was­n’t always so placid. In antiq­ui­ty, rains caused it to flood every year. Sen­a­tor-his­to­ri­an Cas­sius Dio record­ed an inci­dent in 54 BC when the sud­den­ly ris­ing waters caused not just hous­es but whole neigh­bor­hoods to col­lapse. The Tiber’s flood­ing wors­ened over time, inspir­ing Julius Cae­sar to pro­pose re-rout­ing it either around Rome or into a tun­nel run­ning beneath the city. Unfor­tu­nate­ly, the Ides of March came before work could get under­way. Augus­tus opt­ed to dredge the riv­er chan­nel, and Tiberius cham­pi­oned divert­ing its trib­u­taries. Only the con­struc­tion of mod­ern embank­ments in the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry brought the reg­u­lar flu­vial dis­as­ters under con­trol, ensur­ing peace for strollers in search of their own dolce vita.

Roman ships sail­ing to Greece had to make their way around the Pelo­pon­nese, the south of the Greek penin­su­la. The dan­gers of that stretch were many, and did their part to sink the ship car­ry­ing the Antikythera Mech­a­nism. The Isth­mus of Corinth held out the promise of safer pas­sage, at least for those will­ing to drag their laden ships over a bit of land. Dig­ging a canal was, in some sense, the obvi­ous solu­tion, con­sid­ered by both Julius Cae­sar and Caligu­la, but “only Nero was mega­lo­ma­ni­a­cal enough to actu­al­ly begin the project.” A decent amount of progress had been made before anoth­er instance of regi­cide (or per­haps, in this par­tic­u­lar case, tyran­ni­cide) put a stop to the work. Rather than being resumed by a lat­er emper­or, the canal “became a byword for hubris” — at least until the job was final­ly done in the uncom­mon­ly ambi­tious nine­teenth cen­tu­ry.

In cen­tral Ger­many, near where the vil­lage of Wald­girmes is today, Romans found­ed a city with many fea­tures of an impe­r­i­al set­tle­ment, such as a clas­sic street grid, pipes run­ning from a cen­tral aque­duct, and a forum, at the cen­ter of which a gild­ed stat­ue of Augus­tus on horse­back once stood. Dat­ing to the year 4 BC, the city was intend­ed as a new cap­i­tal for what the Romans called Ger­ma­nia, though it end­ed up aban­doned after the Bat­tle of the Teu­to­burg For­est only about a decade after its found­ing. “The build­ings were burned,” Ryan says. “The head of Augus­tus’ eques­tri­an stat­ue was thrown down a well,” only to be dis­cov­ered nine­teen cen­turies lat­er. That image could inspire a med­i­ta­tion on what may be the way of all empires — or serve as a warn­ing to any Amer­i­can leader con­sid­er­ing immor­tal­iz­ing him­self and his horse in gold.

entries.title: Watch “The Midnight Parasites,” a Surreal Japanese Animation Set in the World of Hieronymus Bosch’s The Garden of Earthly Delights (1972)
entries.summary: Hieronymus Bosch’s bizarre paintings might have looked perfectly ordinary to his contemporaries, argues Stanley Meisler in “The World of Bosch.” Modern viewers may find this very hard to believe. We approach Bosch through layers of Freudian interpretation and Surrealist appreciation. We cannot help “regarding the scores of bizarre monsters”—allegories for sins and punishments far more […]
entries.content:
Hierony­mus Bosch’s bizarre paint­ings might have looked per­fect­ly ordi­nary to his con­tem­po­raries, argues Stan­ley Meisler in “The World of Bosch.” Mod­ern view­ers may find this very hard to believe. We approach Bosch through lay­ers of Freudi­an inter­pre­ta­tion and Sur­re­al­ist appre­ci­a­tion. We can­not help “regard­ing the scores of bizarre monsters”—allegories for sins and pun­ish­ments far more leg­i­ble in 15th-cen­tu­ry Netherlands—“as a kind of dark and cru­el com­ic relief.”

While Bosch might have intend­ed his work as seri­ous ser­mo­niz­ing, it is impos­si­ble for us to inhab­it the medieval con­scious­ness of his time and place. There’s just no get­ting around the fact that Bosch is real­ly weird—weird­er even (or more imag­i­na­tive­ly alle­gor­i­cal) than near­ly any oth­er artist of his time. In some very impor­tant ways, he belongs to a 20th-cen­tu­ry aes­thet­ic of post-Freudi­an dream log­ic as much as he belonged to pecu­liar medieval visions of heav­en and hell.

Bosch “described ter­ri­ble, unbear­able holo­causts crush­ing mankind for its sins,” writes Meisler, visions that seemed both stranger and more famil­iar in the wake of so many man-made holo­causts whose absur­di­ties defy rea­son. What mod­ern hor­rors does famed Japan­ese ani­ma­tor Yōji Kuri invoke in his psy­che­del­ic 1972 film “The Mid­night Par­a­sites,” above, a sur­re­al­ist short set in the world of Bosch?

Dan­ger­ous Minds’ Paul Gal­lagher describes the plot, such as it is:

Here Kuri imag­ines what would life might be like if we all lived in Bosch’s paint­ing “Gar­den of Earth­ly Delights.” It’s a basi­cal­ly shit and death or rather a cycle of life where blue fig­ures live and die; eat shit and shit gold; are skew­ered, and devoured; are regur­gi­tat­ed and reborn to car­ry on the cycle once again.

Kuri’s satir­i­cal vision, in films long favored by coun­ter­cul­tur­al audi­ences, has “bite,” writes Ani­ma­tion World Network’s Chris Robin­son: “he helped lift Japan­ese ani­ma­tion out of decades of cozy nar­ra­tive car­toons into a new era of graph­ic and con­cep­tu­al exper­i­men­ta­tion. His films mock and shock, attack­ing tech­nol­o­gy, pop­u­la­tion expan­sion, monot­o­ny of mod­ern soci­ety… Wit­ness­ing the sur­ren­der of Japan dur­ing WW2, the dev­as­ta­tion of his coun­try fol­lowed by the quick rise of West­ern inspired mate­ri­al­ist cul­ture and ram­pant con­sump­tion, Kuri, like many of his col­leagues at the time, ques­tioned the state and direc­tion of his soci­ety and world.”

His cre­ative appro­pri­a­tion of Bosch, “dark, dirty, odd­ly beau­ti­ful, with a groovy sound­track,” Gal­lagher writes, may not, as Meisler wor­ries of many mod­ern takes, get Bosch wrong at all. Though the Dutch artist’s sym­bol­ism may nev­er be comprehensible—or any­thing less than hallucinatory—to us mod­erns, Kuri’s half-play­ful reimag­in­ing uses Boschi­an fig­ures for some seri­ous mor­al­iz­ing, show­ing us a hell world gov­erned by grave laps­es and cru­el­ties Bosch could nev­er have imag­ined.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

entries.title: Why Cleopatra, Lawrence of Arabia, Ben-Hur & Other Hollywood Classics Still Look So Good
entries.summary: Cleopatra cost Twentieth Century Fox $44 million, by the studio’s own estimate. That may sound like the budget of one of those genre pictures that winds up going straight to streaming, but if we convert those 1963 dollars into current ones, it comes out to $480 million. The most expensive film ever made up to […]
entries.content:
Cleopa­tra cost Twen­ti­eth Cen­tu­ry Fox $44 mil­lion, by the stu­dio’s own esti­mate. That may sound like the bud­get of one of those genre pic­tures that winds up going straight to stream­ing, but if we con­vert those 1963 dol­lars into cur­rent ones, it comes out to $480 mil­lion. The most expen­sive film ever made up to that point, it remained an indus­try sym­bol of near-par­o­d­i­cal­ly trou­bled pro­duc­tion and grotesque cost infla­tion for decades. Like The Wiz­ard of Oz, it failed to recoup its invest­ment dur­ing its ini­tial the­atri­cal run, even­tu­al­ly turn­ing a prof­it thanks only to re-releas­es and tele­vi­sion rights sales. And yet, these six decades lat­er, the invest­ment seems to have proven sound, at least accord­ing to the video above from YouTube chan­nel Wolfcrow, “Why Cleopa­tra Still Looks Like a Tril­lion Bucks.”

Unlike some infa­mous­ly expen­sive movies, Cleopa­tra does­n’t leave you won­der­ing where all the mon­ey went. Wolfcrow cre­ator Sareesh Sud­hakaran points out some of the myr­i­ad ways it man­i­fests onscreen, from the 70-foot-long giant sphinx to the full-scale Alexan­dria har­bor built on the coast to the Roman Forum set designed to be three times larg­er than the actu­al Roman Forum to the 65 or so out­fits Eliz­a­beth Tay­lor wears in the title role (to say noth­ing of the 26,000 oth­er cos­tumes made for all the oth­er char­ac­ters). Even the mat­te paint­ings and opti­cal cam­era tricks still look con­vinc­ing. The film’s pro­duc­tion design­ers knew that noth­ing could be done by half mea­sures, giv­en that the 65mm Todd-AO stock used for film­ing would expose any flim­si­ness on the big screen.

Just as unfor­giv­ing was the ultra-wide aspect ratio used for the 1959 ver­sion of Ben-Hur, which neces­si­tat­ed painstak­ing labor on every­thing that went before the cam­era, but also a new approach to the com­po­si­tion of the shots them­selves. Even those of us who’ve nev­er seen the movie can call to mind images of its cli­mac­tic char­i­ot race, a sequence that earned its cul­tur­al impact the hard way.

It took five months to film on the largest set ever built at that time, with 1,500 extras in its stands. A few years lat­er, Lawrence of Ara­bia took Hol­ly­wood grandeur up to the lev­el of sub­lim­i­ty with its real desert land­scapes. David Lean “was obsessed with scale and detail,” Sud­hakaran explains. “He want­ed the desert to be more than just a back­drop. He want­ed it to be a char­ac­ter in the sto­ry,” which required metic­u­lous plan­ning of all the ways its nat­ur­al light could pos­si­bly be used to dra­mat­ic effect.

Though Sud­hakaran clear­ly has an inter­est in spec­ta­cles from the gold­en age of the Hol­ly­wood his­tor­i­cal epics, he’s also made videos on last­ing­ly impres­sive movies from oth­er times and gen­res. When was the last time you sat down to enjoy the satir­i­cal urban tech­no-dystopia Robo­Cop, the com­ic-strip noir fan­ta­sia of Dick Tra­cy, or the flam­boy­ant de-famil­iar­ized twen­ty-third cen­tu­ry of The Fifth Ele­ment — or bet­ter yet, saw them prop­er­ly screened at a revival house? When they came out, those films met with vary­ing degrees of box-office suc­cess and crit­i­cal praise, if not regard­ed as the absolute peak of cin­e­mat­ic sophis­ti­ca­tion. In our time, their ambi­tion and craft look noth­ing short of aston­ish­ing, espe­cial­ly when we remem­ber that they built their worlds in phys­i­cal real­i­ty with real human beings, most­ly ana­log tech­niques, and a whole lot of labor and imag­i­na­tion. Could even a tril­lion dol­lars buy the same results today?

entries.title: Soviet-Era Illustrations of J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit (1976)
entries.summary: Until I read J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, my favorite book growing up was, by far, The Hobbit. Growing up in Russia, however, meant that instead of Tolkien’s English version, my parents read me a Russian translation. To me, the translation easily matched the pace and wonder of Tolkien’s original. Looking […]
entries.content:
Until I read J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, my favorite book grow­ing up was, by far, The Hob­bit. Grow­ing up in Rus­sia, how­ev­er, meant that instead of Tolkien’s Eng­lish ver­sion, my par­ents read me a Russ­ian trans­la­tion. To me, the trans­la­tion eas­i­ly matched the pace and won­der of Tolkien’s orig­i­nal. Look­ing back, The Hob­bit prob­a­bly made such an indeli­ble impres­sion on me because Tolkien’s tale was alto­geth­er dif­fer­ent than the Russ­ian fairy tales and children’s sto­ries that I had pre­vi­ous­ly been exposed to. There were no child­ish hijinks, no young pro­tag­o­nists, no par­ents to res­cue you when you got into trou­ble. I con­sid­ered it an epic in the truest lit­er­ary sense.

As with many Russ­ian trans­la­tions dur­ing the Cold War, the book came with a com­plete­ly dif­fer­ent set of illus­tra­tions. Mine, I remem­ber regret­ting slight­ly, lacked pic­tures alto­geth­er. A friend’s edi­tion, how­ev­er, was illus­trat­ed in the typ­i­cal Russ­ian style: much more tra­di­tion­al­ly styl­ized than Tolkien’s own draw­ings, they were more angu­lar, friend­lier, almost car­toon­ish. In this post, we include a num­ber of these images from the 1976 print­ing. The cov­er, above, depicts a grin­ning Bil­bo Bag­gins hold­ing a gem. Below, Gan­dalf, an osten­si­bly harm­less soul, pays Bil­bo a vis­it.

Next, we have the three trolls, argu­ing about their var­i­ous eat­ing arrange­ments, with Bil­bo hid­ing to the side.

Here, Gol­lum, né Sméagol, pad­dles his raft in the depths of the moun­tains.

Final­ly, here’s Bil­bo, ful­fill­ing his role as a bur­glar in Smaug’s lair.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2014.

Ilia Blin­d­er­man is a Mon­tre­al-based cul­ture and sci­ence writer.

entries.title: The Names of Nearly 4 Million Enslaved People in Former British Colonies Are Now Searchable Online, Helping Descendants Find Lost Ancestors
entries.summary: A few years ago, we featured here on Open Culture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project database, which contains searchable information on formerly enslaved people in the United States after its Civil War. With nearly 1.8 million men, women, and children registered there when it first opened to the public, it has remained a valuable resource for […]
entries.content:
A few years ago, we fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture the Freedmen’s Bureau Project data­base, which con­tains search­able infor­ma­tion on for­mer­ly enslaved peo­ple in the Unit­ed States after its Civ­il War. With near­ly 1.8 mil­lion men, women, and chil­dren reg­is­tered there when it first opened to the pub­lic, it has remained a valu­able resource for many Amer­i­cans research­ing their own her­itage, not just descen­dants of for­mer slaves but of oth­er Civ­il War refugees as well. But of course, the U.S. was hard­ly the only coun­try where slav­ery exist­ed. Count­less peo­ple here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry have ances­tors who were enslaved in oth­er for­mer British colonies, and now they’ve got a por­tal through which to do genealog­i­cal search­es of their own.

Launched by a part­ner­ship between the geneal­o­gy com­pa­ny Ances­try and the Cen­tre for the Study of the Lega­cies of British Slav­ery at Uni­ver­si­ty Col­lege Lon­don, the online For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters makes avail­able records on near­ly four mil­lion indi­vid­u­als enslaved between 1813 and 1840 in a host of coun­tries from the Bahamas to Mau­ri­tius to South Africa.

First cre­at­ed by the British gov­ern­ment dur­ing the process of abol­ish­ing the transat­lantic slave trade in 1807 — much as the Freedmen’s Bureau orga­nized its reg­istry of for­mer slaves dur­ing Recon­struc­tion under Abra­ham Lin­coln — the orig­i­nal papers con­tain not just their names and ages, but also mater­nal fam­i­ly con­nec­tions, phys­i­cal descrip­tions, and some­times details about their place of African ori­gin.

In the video above, geneal­o­gist and Ances­try Senior Sto­ry Pro­duc­er Nic­ka Sewell-Smith pro­vides an intro­duc­tion to the For­mer British Colonies Enslave­ment Reg­is­ters, which you can access here. If you’re curi­ous about whether your own ances­tors may appear in its records, you can search by details like name, approx­i­mate date, or loca­tion to nar­row down the poten­tial match­es. The mod­ern descen­dants of peo­ple enslaved in the 20 coun­tries cov­ered by the data­base by no means live exclu­sive­ly, or even pri­mar­i­ly, in those coun­tries or in Great Britain itself. More than two cen­turies lat­er, their descen­dants live all over the world, includ­ing in Latin Amer­i­ca and the Unit­ed States, lead­ing lives very dif­fer­ent from those of their enslaved ances­tors — but the recon­struc­tion of their fam­i­ly sto­ries has only just begun. Enter the data­base here.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

entries.title: The Bialetti Moka Express: The History of Italy’s Iconic Coffee Maker, and How to Use It the Right Way
entries.summary: I am sure that many an Open Culture reader has a Bialetti Moka Express in their kitchen. I know I do, but I must add that I knew little about its history and apparently even less about how to properly use one. Coffee expert and author of The World Atlas of Coffee James Hoffmann introduces […]
entries.content:
I am sure that many an Open Cul­ture read­er has a Bialet­ti Moka Express in their kitchen. I know I do, but I must add that I knew lit­tle about its his­to­ry and appar­ent­ly even less about how to prop­er­ly use one. Cof­fee expert and author of The World Atlas of Cof­fee James Hoff­mann intro­duces us to the appli­ance we think we know in the above video.

Alfon­so Bialet­ti didn’t orig­i­nal­ly get into the cof­fee busi­ness. In 1919, the Bialet­ti com­pa­ny was an alu­minum man­u­fac­tur­er, with the Moka Express invent­ed some­where around 1933 by Lui­gi de Pon­ti, who worked for the com­pa­ny. Accord­ing to Decon­struct­ing Prod­uct Design by William Lid­well and Ger­ry Man­ac­sa, the inspi­ra­tion came from Bialetti’s wife’s old-fash­ioned wash­ing machine: “a fire, a buck­et, and a lid with a tube com­ing out of it. The buck­et was filled with soapy water, sealed with the lid, and then brought to a boil over the fire, at which point the vapor­ized soapy water was pushed up through the tube and expelled on to the laun­dry.”

As Hoff­mann shows, ear­li­er cof­fee-mak­ers did use steam and a drip tech­nique, but the Moka Express was the first all-in-one mak­er that could sit on the stove top and do the work. All the user had to lis­ten for was the tell-tale gur­gle when it fin­ished brew­ing.

In 1945, Alfonso’s son Rena­to returned from a pris­on­er-of-war camp and took over the fam­i­ly busi­ness. He was instru­men­tal in focus­ing on the Moka Express and turn­ing it into an inter­na­tion­al cof­fee brand. He hired car­toon­ist Paul Cam­pani to design l’omino coi baf­fi, “the mus­ta­chioed lit­tle man” whose image is on the side of every Moka Express, and who, dur­ing the 1950s, was in a series of humor­ous ani­mat­ed com­mer­cials. Bialet­ti was the pride of Italy, and for Ital­ian immi­grants liv­ing abroad, it was a trea­sured object in the kitchen.

Such was the iden­ti­fi­ca­tion of Rena­to Bialet­ti with the Moka Express that when he died in 2016, his ash­es were interred in a giant repli­ca pot. Hoff­mann details the fate of the com­pa­ny after­wards, how it has fared against com­peti­tors in Italy and out­side. Will it still be around in decades? Who knows. But it does make a great cup of cof­fee.

And he shows the cor­rect way to brew a cup with the Moka Express in this oth­er video. Here are a few things I was doing wrong: not using hot water in the bot­tom to start; try­ing to pack in the ground cof­fee like I was mak­ing an espres­so; using too fine a grind; and not cool­ing the bot­tom as soon as it’s done work­ing its mag­ic. (Note: a Moka Express cof­fee is some­where between an espres­so and a pour-over.) All these tips I’m going to try tomor­row morn­ing. Maybe you have been mak­ing your Bialet­ti cup the right way all along. Let me know in the com­ments. I’ll read them over a fresh­ly brewed cup.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2022.
